item.title: PB Fintech, Turtlemint Shares Rally Up To 8% After IRDAI Forms Reforms Review Panel
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Update | November 25, 19:49 IST Turtlemint’s shares closed the trading session 3.17% higher at ₹1,124.60 apiece on the BSE.…
item.content:encoded:
Update | November 25, 19:49 IST

Turtlemint’s shares closed the trading session 3.17% higher at ₹1,124.60 apiece on the BSE. Meanwhile, Turtlemint’s shares closed at the 5% upper circuit.

Original| November 25, 12:15 IST

Shares of Policybazaar parent PB Fintech jumped 7.9% to an intraday high of ₹1,176.3 apiece on the BSE today, while Turtlemint hit its 5% upper circuit at ₹67.9.

The rally followed the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India’s (IRDAI) decision to constitute a six-member expert committee to review feedback on its proposed insurance distribution reforms, which have weighed on both stocks over the past two months.

PB Fintech subsequently pared some gains, trading 3.3% higher at ₹1,125.6 apiece at 11:33 IST. Turtlemint remained at its upper circuit at 11:37 AM IST.

IRDAI’s committee will be chaired by Indu Bhushan, former IAS officer and founding CEO of Ayushman Bharat. It has until December 31 to submit its recommendations.

IRDAI said it received about 2.18 Lakh responses to 32 questions from more than 13,000 participants by the extended October 31 deadline. The proposals cover distribution structures, commissions, expenses of management (EoM), market conduct, transparency, and digital infrastructure.

The committee will examine whether the reforms could adversely affect employment and the incomes of insurance agents and other distributors, and recommend measures to mitigate any impact. It will also consider phased implementation and other transition arrangements for smaller distributors and insurers.

Its members include NCAER director general Suresh Goyal, former Oriental Insurance CMD A.V. Girija Kumar, former Howden Insurance Brokers India CEO and chairman Praveen Vashishta, and former SBI Life MD and CEO Mahesh Kumar Sharma. IRDAI executive director Ayyaj Tamboli is the convenor.

Distribution Economics Under Review

IRDAI’s September 23 consultation paper, ‘Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution’, proposed product-wise commission caps and tighter limits on insurers’ expenses of management (EoM).

The regulator argued that payouts have outpaced premium growth since distribution rules were relaxed in 2023, without a corresponding improvement in insurance coverage.

The proposals triggered a sell-off on September 24, when PB Fintech fell 36% and Turtlemint hit its 20% lower circuit. Lower payouts could squeeze the commission pool available to these platforms and their distribution partners.

These concerns extend across the industry. The Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) has warned of a 60-70% decline in broking revenues and risks to up to 10 Lakh jobs.

The association said the distribution sector employs over 83 Lakh people, with smaller businesses and MSMEs particularly vulnerable. Job losses could also weaken policy renewals, policyholder assistance, and insurance penetration.

IBAI disputed IRDAI’s data showing broker-sourced general insurance premiums grew 37%, while commissions increased 173%, between FY23 and FY25. It attributed much of the increase to previously off-book marketing expenses being reclassified following regularisation.

It also claimed insurers’ operating expenses averaged 26.5% of gross premiums, below the 30% limit. Policyholders received ₹84.4 in claims per ₹100 of non-life premiums over five years, against a global average of 72–75%, it said.

IBAI has sought intervention from the Prime Minister’s Office and finance ministry, while offering to address mis-selling and disproportionate remuneration.

Brokerages Weigh Earnings Impact

Following IRDAI’s move to set up the review panel, Jefferies outlined potential earnings outcomes for PB Fintech depending on changes to the proposed commission rules.

Its moderate scenario assumes higher commissions on new health policies and lower costs, putting PB Fintech’s FY30 profit after tax 25% above its worst-case estimate.

A more favourable scenario involving higher health and life commissions could lift PAT by 40%. If the initial proposal remains unchanged, FY30 PAT could be 39% below its pre-regulation estimate.

Morgan Stanley maintained an ‘attractive’ industry view, highlighting possible mitigation measures, including phased implementation for smaller distributors. It said insurers remain better positioned than distributors and stayed positive on life insurers.

Motilal Oswal Financial Services said the reforms could prompt insurers to rethink distribution and cut costs, following changes including surrender value regulations and the GST waiver.

item.title: Fintech Unicorn Oxyzo Posts 19% Rise In H1 FY27 Profit To ₹208 Cr
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Oxyzo Financial Services, the lending arm of OfBusiness, reported a 19% increase in standalone net profit to ₹208.2 Cr in…
item.content:encoded:
Oxyzo Financial Services, the lending arm of OfBusiness, reported a 19% increase in standalone net profit to ₹208.2 Cr in the first half of FY27 from ₹174.9 Cr in the corresponding period last year.

Revenue from operations grew 28.4% to ₹874.9 Cr in H1 FY27 from ₹681.2 Cr. Interest income remained the biggest contributor, rising 31.7% to ₹859.0 Cr from ₹652.5 Cr.

However, fee and commission income declined 23.1% to ₹14.4 Cr from ₹18.7 Cr.

On a consolidated basis, Oxyzo’s operating revenue increased 31.0% to ₹910 Cr in the six months ended September 2026, while net profit rose 27% to ₹218 Cr, as per consolidated statements accessed by Inc42.

Interest income contributed ₹866.2 Cr to consolidated operating revenue, while fee and commission income stood at ₹36.2 Cr.

For Q2 FY27, Oxyzo’s standalone operating revenue increased 30.3% to ₹445.5 Cr from ₹341.9 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Standalone net profit grew 25.1% to ₹108.7 Cr from ₹86.9 Cr.

Loan Book Expands Further

In a statement, Oxyzo said its consolidated assets grew 38% to ₹13,289 Cr at September-end. Its loan book expanded 33.6% to ₹11,531 Cr from ₹8,631 Cr a year earlier.

Gross non-performing assets (GNPA) stood at 0.8%, while net non-performing assets (NNPA) were 0.3%.

The NBFC reported a return on assets of 3.6%, a debt-to-equity ratio of 2.7X, and a capital adequacy ratio of 28.0%.

For comparison, Oxyzo ended FY26 with a loan book of ₹10,545 Cr, gross NPA of 0.7%, and net NPA of 0.3%. Its capital adequacy ratio stood at 29.0% at March-end.

The company said it maintained a diversified borrowing mix across banks, NBFCs, and capital markets. Its lenders include SBI, Federal Bank, IndusInd Bank, IDFC FIRST Bank, Axis Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank, and SIDBI, among others.

Where Did Oxyzo Spend In H1 FY27? 

The NBFC’s standalone total expenses grew 33.1% to ₹594.9 Cr in H1 FY27 from ₹446.9 Cr in the year-ago period. 

Finance Costs: This was the largest expense component, increasing 35% to ₹378.2 Cr from ₹2801 Cr.

Employee Benefit Expenses: Expenditure under this head rose 42.1% to ₹90.7 Cr from ₹63.8 Cr.

Impairment Expenses: This cost head increased 36.6% to ₹62.9 Cr from ₹46.1 Cr.

Expanding Beyond SME Lending

Founded in 2016 by Ashish Mohapatra, Bhuvan Gupta, Ruchi Kalra, and Vasant Sridhar, Oxyzo provides loans to SMEs in the manufacturing and contracting sectors. These include financing for raw materials, machinery, and working capital requirements.

Beyond core lending, the company is expanding into debt investment and fund management to serve SME customers and emerging corporates.

Oxyzo recently acquired debt investment and bond distribution platform GoldenPi to strengthen its debt capital markets business. In May, its board approved the acquisition of GoldenPi Technologies and its wholly owned subsidiary GoldenPi Securities through a share-swap deal valued at ₹42.4 Cr. 

Earlier this year, it also launched Oxyzo Credit Fund I, a performing credit fund under its alternative investment platform.

Registered with SEBI as a Category II alternative investment fund (AIF), the fund provides secured credit to mid-sized, investment-grade companies seeking growth capital. It is managed by Oxyzo Investment Manager, a wholly owned subsidiary of the NBFC.

item.title: The Growing Toll Of Token Frauds
item.dc:creator: Ankush Das
item.description: A new breed of fraudsters is taking the AI world by storm. But rather than stealing money or data, they…
item.content:encoded:
A new breed of fraudsters is taking the AI world by storm. But rather than stealing money or data, they have found a way to make businesses and AI users cough up tokens for them. 

Welcome to the murky world of AI token fraud or LLM-jacking, where attackers steal API keys, cloud credentials or other access tokens to use paid AI models and sometimes resell that access. 

But stolen credentials are just the tip of the iceberg. From free credits and promotional offers to stolen credit cards and publicly accessible AI tools, fraudsters are exploiting multiple avenues to access AI resources at someone else’s expense.

For AI startups, this makes cybersecurity as much a financial challenge as a technological one. Bad actors and criminals no longer need to steal sensitive data or cripple infrastructure to inflict serious damage. Simply running up a company’s AI bill can burn a hole in its balance sheet by driving up inference costs.

So, how are criminals turning AI access into a money-making machine? How big a dent can token fraud leave? And what are businesses doing to plug these loopholes? We spoke to industry leaders to unpack the economics of AI token fraud in this edition of The AI Shift. Let’s dive in…

AI’s Million-Dollar Free Ride

A November 2026 investigation by Google found that several organisations hit by LLM-jacking incurred more than $100K in fraudulent cloud charges in a single day. For some, the total bill reached $1 Mn before they could stop the abuse.

In one instance, fraudsters used stolen credentials to access paid AI models more than 500,000 times in less than eight hours, leaving the victim to bear the cost of processing those requests. What’s more, fraudsters are not just using stolen AI access for themselves but also selling it to others. 

Google calls these illegal intermediaries “LLM Mixers”, which essentially make money by selling AI services that someone else is paying for.

What makes some of these fraudulent activities difficult to detect is that unauthorised AI usage can initially look like regular customer activity, allowing costs to mount before businesses realise something is amiss. 

Here it’s important to know that stealing credentials is not the only way to exploit AI companies.

Reuben Koh, director of security technology and strategy for Asia Pacific and Japan at cybersecurity company Akamai, said the company is witnessing a phenomenon called “AI token freeloading”, where fraudsters use a company’s publicly accessible AI chatbots or search tools to process their own workloads. 

While each request may cost the company very little, thousands of such requests can collectively result in a hefty AI bill without triggering any security alerts.

But in its blog, Google added, “While low-level resource theft has involved the manipulation of customer support chatbots to conduct unauthorised tasks like code generation, threat actors conducting LLMJacking bypass these front-end interfaces to target backend model resources directly.” 

The latter can result in a significant loss for the company. “Leaving these services unprotected not only expands an organisation’s traditional attack surface, but could also introduce a significant increase in hosting costs,” the company said.

The Free Trial Trap

Some ways that criminals lure in businesses include free trials, promotional credits and generous discounts. These have long been part of the startup playbook for acquiring customers in the early stages. 

But in the AI economy, where every user interaction can come with a compute cost, these growth levers are turning into a double-edged sword.

Criminals or bad actors can leverage the very incentives that startups offer to drive adoption to execute their agenda.

A case in point is AI infrastructure startup JarvisLabs. Cofounder Vishnu Subramanian revealed that the startup repeatedly encountered abuse when it offered free credits. 

“Every time we offered free credits, people showed up to mine crypto on our GPUs,” Subramanian said, adding that stolen cards created another problem, with users consuming compute credits knowing fully well that payment disputes will only surface weeks later. 

With AI inference, he expects the same incentive to appear in a different form, with free tokens potentially being resold instead. 

JarvisLabs addressed much of this through compliance, by adding a security layer to online card payments to verify cardholders and reduce fraud. This increased the friction, particularly for customers in developed markets, but the company is happy accepting the trade-off because it reduced stolen-card usage and disputes.

A problem of a similar nature is emerging among AI application companies. Claire Vo, founder of product management AI platform ChatPRD, wrote in a blog post that token fraud had cost her bootstrapped business tens of thousands of dollars in a year. 

The company encountered trial farming, promotional-code abuse, card fraud and resellers routing requests through its product. ChatPRD eventually shut down free trials after such abuse did not stop, even when the company required a credit card on record.

Here companies need to understand that every request in an AI product can carry a direct inference bill, particularly on expensive frontier models. And to their credit most companies do, but experts believe that keeping a close eye on free credits and trials is important to protect their business. 

Securing AI’s Many Front Doors

For Indian AI startups and enterprises, the response to token heists or fraud may be to move beyond conventional cybersecurity controls and see how existing processes create barriers in an AI-first world.

Koh of Akamai said organisations should tie access credentials to specific applications and models, impose hard spending limits and alerts, and replace permanent credentials with temporary ones..  

They should also monitor small probing requests, unexpected models and unusual geographic usage. For public-facing AI features, he recommends bot management and per-session usage limits before requests reach the underlying model.

Google’s investigation points to a similar shift, with attackers exploiting cloud credentials, API keys and exposed AI endpoints. The tech giant expects the threat to grow as enterprises embed AI agents and third-party AI infrastructure in their workflows.

Ketan Ramshawala, cofounder and CTO of cybersecurity and fintech company Synctric, believes banks and NBFCs need to treat API credentials and access limits as another attack surface. Organisations should monitor real-time traffic, set limits on API usage and act on unusual activity rather than letting repeated security alerts become background noise.

He also stressed the need to control how credentials are stored and accessed. Applying usage thresholds based on a customer’s transaction patterns, including automatically disabling APIs outside expected operating windows, can mitigate some of the risk. 

The bigger problem is that an AI company rarely has just one door anymore. As AI becomes more deeply embedded in enterprise workflows, the risks will only multiply. A typical AI application today relies on multiple model providers, cloud infrastructure partners, third-party APIs and payment gateways. 

Each such integration creates another potential avenue for abuse. And that’s why it is vital for every business to understand its own AI supply chain. There’s no one solution that will work for every company. 

Going forward, fraud prevention is likely to become an integral part of the first principles work that goes into building an AI product, rather than remaining the sole responsibility of the cybersecurity team. 

User engagement undoubtedly also plays a role in how investors view AI companies, particularly those at the early stage. So it’s all the more important that companies get this right, or risk failing due diligence. 

The Weekly Buzz: Nvidia Brings Jensen Huang Back As CEO

Just 11 days after his resignation, Nvidia’s board voted unanimously this week to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as the president, CEO and director. The board said it consulted senior US government officials and concluded his return posed no national security risk.

Shares jumped sharply on the news, surging as much as 33% and adding hundreds of billions in market value as investors welcomed the return of the company’s longtime leader. Huang’s brief exit rattled the entire AI sector, given Nvidia’s dominant role in supplying the chips that power frontier models. Reports indicated political pressure, including from the White House, played a role in accelerating the decision.

The reinstatement stabilises the most important company in the AI infrastructure stack at a moment of intense competition and regulatory scrutiny. Huang is expected to address Congress in the coming days as questions about the circumstances of his departure continue.

Top Stories From India & Around The World

  • Matters.AI Raises ₹115 Cr: The AI-native data security startup has raised ₹115 Cr ($12 Mn) in a pre-Series A round. Matters will use the fresh inflow of funds to accelerate product development and expand its operations in North America.
  • Sarvam Defends Token Factory: The Indian AI giant said its Token Factory runs on privately procured GPUs and reiterated that building homegrown AI models remains its core focus amid questions over hosting global open-weight models.
  • Scaler Cofounder Launches Arcfront: Anshuman Singh has launched an AI research and training data startup with former Scaler AI executive Naman Bhalla to build specialised training data for frontier AI labs and model developers.
  • Disseqt AI Raises $8 Mn: The AI governance startup has raised $8 Mn from Gresham House Ventures and other investors to expand its enterprise customer base and international operations as AI agent adoption grows.

Startup In The Spotlight: VerifAIX

Founded in 2024 by Madhulima Tewari and Kenneth Roe, VerifAIX is building an AI-powered verification platform designed to help chipmakers test and validate increasingly complex hardware faster.

Chip verification can consume months of development time as engineers check whether every component behaves according to its specifications. The challenge is becoming more pronounced as AI is increasingly used to generate hardware designs and verification code, creating a need for independent systems that can validate whether those outputs are correct.

VerifAIX has developed a “Formal Brain” that creates a grounded model of a chip using its specifications, RTL code and existing verification assets. Its agentic AI platform then uses this model to generate verification plans, testbenches, assertions and coverage workflows, while checking whether the chip design aligns with its original specifications.

The startup has raised $5 Mn in seed funding and is targeting the global electronic design automation market, which is projected to reach $35.6 Bn by 2034. VerifAIX competes with established EDA players such as Synopsys, Cadence and Siemens while focusing on using AI to make chip verification faster and more automated.

Prompt Of The Week

What prompts and hacks are CTOs, CEOs and cofounders using these days to streamline their work? 

Here’s Shivam Mani Tripathi, cofounder and CTO at Privyr, with a prompt he uses to help salespeople turn a new WhatsApp enquiry into a meaningful conversation.

“I am the cofounder and CTO of Privyr, a mobile-first CRM for sales teams who sell over WhatsApp and phone. I’m not an expert content writer.

Our leads come from Facebook and Instagram ads, landing pages and WhatsApp. The first reply often determines whether a lead continues or goes cold.

Think like an experienced conversion copywriter who understands how Indian salespeople communicate on WhatsApp.

Lead details: [Source, enquiry, first message, language]

No AI fluff or AI tells. Write like a busy salesperson typing on a phone. No em dashes, “not X but Y”, lists of three, hype or sign-offs.

Rules:

– Under 40 words per reply.

– Match the lead’s language and tone.

– Keep it natural and lock-screen friendly.

– Never invent facts or pricing promises.

– Ask one question per message.

– Don’t sound like a qualification checklist.

First replies: Write three alternatives. Identify what’s known and unknown using BANT (budget, authority, need, timeline). Where possible, explore different unknowns through natural questions. Briefly explain each approach.

Voice note: Turn the strongest reply into a natural 15-second WhatsApp voice-note script.

Reusable playbook: Explain what stays consistent and what changes across leads. Create a swipe file of adaptable openers and discovery questions.

Keep everything practical and ready to use. Avoid generic sales advice.”

Editor’s Note: Some prompts may need to be adjusted by users for best results or may not work as intended for certain users.

[Edited by Shishir Parasher]

item.content:encoded:
JioStar’s Second Round Of Layoffs

Layoffs hit two major pillars of India’s digital economy this week. Media giant JioStar is trimming at least 150 jobs, while Google Cloud India confirmed that it slashed around 30 roles last week. But why are corporate giants laying off teams even as digital demand climbs?

JioStar Draws Its Axe: Barely 18 months after cutting over 1,000 roles following the Viacom18-Star India merger, JioStar is initiating a second round of layoffs that will impact roles across marketing, production, studios and operations. Sources suggest that the final number could be higher than 150. The latest layoffs reflect mounting profitability pressures at the media giant. 

JioStar’s Margin Pressure: The media giant’s financials tell a more complicated story. Despite higher revenue and viewership, margins are shrinking – Q2 FY27 EBITDA fell 11% YoY and margins contracted 600 bps. At the same time, JioStar is investing in content, sports rights and international expansion. This expansion spree appears to have taken a toll on its finances and raised questions over whether its growth is translating into profits.

Google Cloud Downsizes: Hyperscaler Google Cloud has also confirmed that it eliminated nearly 30 roles in India last week, calling it a “small organisational change” amid a reprioritisation of work. The company rejected rumours of large-scale layoffs but did not disclose impacted teams or functions. 

A Broader Wave: JioStar and Google Cloud are not alone in trimming their workforces. Oracle, PayPal, Amazon and Uber all announced job cuts in India in recent months, reportedly impacting more than 3,500 roles. 

Besides this, Microsoft and Google have both rolled out voluntary exit plans for employees instead of resorting to layoffs. This reflects a broader push across the tech ecosystem to control costs, restructure teams and redirect spending towards AI and automation. 

As questions remain over whether these big giants can build sustainable businesses without repeatedly shrinking their workforces, here is all about the JioStar layoff saga…

From The Editor’s Desk

AidenAI Nets $32 Mn

  • The enterprise AI startup has raised nearly ₹297 Cr in its Series A round led by A91 Partners to bolster its tech stack and engineering capabilities. It also plans to build a team of more than 1,000 frontier AI engineers through its AidenAI Builder Academy.
  • Founded in 2023, the startup helps large enterprises integrate AI into existing apps, data infrastructure and business workflows. It also offers an AI-driven platform that helps businesses modernise legacy software systems.
  • The fundraise comes as enterprises increasingly explore agentic AI applications to automate workflows and streamline operations. On the back of this, the Indian enterprise AI market is projected to become a $71 Bn opportunity by 2030.

Turtlemint Under GST Radar

  • Maharashtra GST authorities are conducting searches at the registered office of the insurance tech company’s subsidiary, Turtlemint Insurance Broking Services, in Mumbai. The search and seizure operation is currently underway. 
  • Turtlemint said that the searches were conducted under Section 67 of the Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017. However, it did not disclose the specific alleged violations or a tax demand. 
  • Founded in 2015, Turtlemint operates an omnichannel insurance distribution platform that enables over 6.6 Lakh financial advisors to sell motor, health, and life insurance. This comes less than five months after the company listed on the exchanges in June.

Shadowfax To Acquire Borzo

  • The listed logistics platform is acquiring the Indian arm of Borzo (formerly WeFast) for ₹23.3 Cr. The deal will enable Shadowfax to enter the on-demand intra-city goods transportation category and expand its reach.
  • Founded in 2012, Borzo operates a fleet of over 32,000 delivery partners across five Indian cities and claims to fulfil over 1.2 Cr deliveries annually. It relocated its base from Amsterdam to Mumbai in 2024 and closed CY25 with an adjusted top line of ₹200 Cr.
  • This acquisition comes as the listed startup looks to build on the traction of its D2C-focused Shadowfax 360 offering and strong growth in its hyperlocal business to broaden its full-stack logistics platform.

GalaxEye’s Mission Drishti

  • The spacetech startup has awarded a multi-year contract to Bellatrix Aerospace. Under this, Bellatrix will design, build and deliver its Arka Hall-effect electric propulsion systems for GalaxEye’s 30 Drishti Gen-II satellites.
  • Under the phased schedule, deliveries will begin with propulsion systems for the first two satellites and will subsequently be scaled to 30. The satellites will be part of an OptoSAR constellation that GalaxEye aims to deploy by 2030.
  • Founded in 2021, GalaxEye combines optical imaging and synthetic aperture radar on a single satellite. Its OptoSAR technology supports Earth observation through clouds and at night for defence and agriculture use cases. It has raised $27 Mn to date.

Former Sequoia Exec’s New AI Bet

  • Former Sequoia India investor Sudhanshu Mishra has launched an agentic AI startup called Demi.AI in the US. The platform is currently in beta mode and is available for a select few users.
  • The new venture will look to build an AI assistant that can anticipate users’ requirements and complete work before being explicitly instructed. Its individual paid plan starts at $25 per month, while team pricing comes with a customised price tag.
  • Mishra worked on early-stage investments at Sequoia India, primarily leading the VC firm’s crypto-focused efforts. He subsequently joined Paradigm, a crypto-focused investment firm, as an investment partner.

item.title: Most Consumer Platforms Rife With Dark Patterns Despite Regulatory Action: Survey
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Nearly three-quarters of consumer companies that declared themselves free of dark patterns to the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) continue…
item.content:encoded:
Nearly three-quarters of consumer companies that declared themselves free of dark patterns to the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) continue to deploy deceptive user-interface practices, despite fresh regulations against such practices set to take effect on January 1.

A study commissioned by LocalCircles analysed 354 widely used online platforms across 45 sectors, drawing on consumer complaints, social media reports and the company’s AI-powered dark pattern detection engine.

The number of companies submitting self-declarations to the CCPA rose to 31 in November from 23 in July. However, platforms operated by 23 of these companies (74%) still contained dark patterns, the study found.

Across the broader sample, 94% of platforms, or 334 out of 354, exhibited at least one dark pattern. Only 20 platforms were found to be free of such practices.

Listed companies fared no better. Of the 108 consumer-facing platforms operated by companies listed on Indian stock exchanges, 102 (94%) continued to feature dark patterns.

In 37 of the 45 sectors examined, not a single platform was found to be compliant. These included online grocery, food delivery, online banking, taxi aggregators, OTT streaming and edtech.

B2B business marketplaces were the only category to achieve 100% compliance, followed by car rental platforms, where compliance stood at 25%. Sectors directly covered by anti-dark pattern protections also recorded low compliance rates. Ecommerce platforms had a compliance rate of just 17%, while quick commerce stood at 14%.

Forced action was the most prevalent dark pattern, appearing on 237 platforms (67%). Drip pricing was the second most common, at 63%, followed by bait and switch (50%) and interface interference (48%).

New Dark Pattern Rules Soon To Come Into Effect

The findings come ahead of the implementation of the Consumer Protection (Ecommerce) (Amendment) Rules, 2026, notified by the Department of Consumer Affairs in September.

The amended rules require ecommerce entities to:

  • Comply with dark pattern guidelines and conduct annual self-audits.
  • Prominently display a ‘dark-pattern-free’ compliance certificate.
  • Disclose the lowest price offered in the preceding 30 days when advertising discounts.
  • Avoid misleading search manipulation and clearly identify sponsored listings
  • Refrain from bundling fees for unrelated services.
  • Obtain express, affirmative consent for specified uses of consumer data.
  • Disclose product details, including ‘best before’ or ‘use before’ dates, along with relevant seller information.
  • Clearly provide return and refund policies, warranty information, delivery terms and payment details.

The findings also build on concerns raised during previous festive sales. We had reported last year on how dark patterns proliferated across ecommerce platforms during festive sales, nudging shoppers towards higher spending and purchases without adequate information.

Since the introduction of regulations prohibiting dark patterns, the CCPA has penalised several platforms, including IndiGo, Zepto, FirstCry, PhysicsWallah, BookMyShow, SpiceJet and Rapido, for deploying such practices.

Sectoral regulators, including the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), have also moved to strengthen consumer protections against dark patterns.
